generation_metadata.title: Fury and Helplessness Rising
generation_metadata.instruction: You're in an elevator with a coworker when you get a phone call—your teenager has been arrested. You answer, trying to stay composed: 'What? Where?' Your voice is controlled, professional, aware of the witness. But as details emerge (you're hearing them, we're not), your composure cracks. Your voice rises, shaking: 'They did WHAT to him?' Rage floods through you—protective, fierce, helpless. You're yelling now: 'I don't care about their procedures! He's sixteen!' But then something in what you hear deflates you completely. Your voice drops to broken: 'Was he scared? Did he ask for me?' Let the fury collapse into devastation. You're trying not to sob in front of this stranger: 'I should have been there. I should have...' The elevator reaches the lobby and you have to pull yourself together enough to run out, but your voice cracks on the final words to the coworker: 'I have to go. My baby needs me.' Exit in pieces, held together only by the urgency of love.

parts.text:
You are a skilled dialogue writer for naturalistic, close-microphone voice acting.
Write a short first-person monologue that could be spoken in a real situation. The actor is
speaking to another person or themselves, not reciting a plot synopsis. Preserve the
challenge's specific situation and emotional development while avoiding melodrama,
generic motivational language, exposition dumps, and perfect studio-script polish.
Human emotion is mixed, context-dependent, and gradually changing. Include small,
credible imperfections or micro-distractions only when they fit. Spoken text should
have about 58-68 words, normally four to six sentences, so that a natural performance
takes roughly 26-32 seconds. Use punctuation, ellipses, and occasional exclamation
points only where the thought calls for them. Never write stage directions in brackets
or in the spoken text: Gemini 3.8 TTS will read all ordinary words aloud.
Use only documented inline tags for momentary human vocal events. No music, foley,
or background sound tags. Do not overuse vocal tags. English dialogue only for this
controlled pilot. Keep profanity and graphic content out of the script.

Respond ONLY as a JSON object with keys:
  spoken_text: a single verbatim transcript including optional inline vocal tags;
  beat_styles: an array of one to three brief English delivery directions, in order;
  intended_emotions: one to three of the 40 EmoNet emotion labels if known, otherwise
    concise ordinary emotion words;
  scene_note: one sentence on why the vocal choice fits the challenge.
